input:
This appraisal considers a proposed warehouse extension with an installed cost of $1313k, which is expected to generate net savings of $374k per year over a period of 8 years. In order to assess the financial viability of the proposal, the expected savings have been discounted at a rate of 6%, giving a present value of $2322k. When the installed cost of $1313k is deducted from this figure, the resulting net present value is $1009k, which is positive and therefore indicates that the project creates value on the basis of the assumptions adopted.

It is important to note, however, that the savings of $374k per year are derived from vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. This means that the net present value of $1009k is ultimately dependent on estimates that have not been validated in practice, and the actual outcome could potentially differ from the appraised outcome if the realised savings turn out to be lower than expected. Nevertheless, the margin between the present value of the savings ($2322k) and the installed cost is substantial, representing a surplus of $1009k, and on this basis the extension can be regarded as a financially attractive proposition, provided that the discount rate of 6% is accepted as appropriate for a commitment of this nature and the 8-year appraisal horizon is considered reasonable in the circumstances.
target:
The warehouse extension clears its appraisal: at a discount rate of 6%, the net present value is $1009k on an installed cost of $1313k. The extension is expected to return net savings of $374k per year for 8 years. Discounted at 6%, those savings have a present value of $2322k, and the excess over the installed cost is the $1009k net present value stated above.

The trade-off stands in one comparison: $2322k of discounted savings against $1313k of installed cost, a surplus of $1009k before any allowance for estimation error. Nothing is counted beyond the 8 years over which the savings are claimed, and the surplus is wide enough that the conclusion does not turn on small movements in the discount rate.

The qualification is the evidence behind the savings. The $374k per year is built from vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. The figure is therefore derived from estimates, and it is stated as such: the appraisal supports the extension on estimated savings, and the decision rests on whether that estimate basis is accepted for the commitment. That is not a defect in the appraisal method; it is the condition of appraising savings that have not yet occurred on an installation that has not yet been built, and it is priced into the decision only if the decision-maker treats the figure as an estimate throughout.
